There is no mechanical forced-selling dynamic available here, and this is the part of the setup that most clearly argues against waiting for a wash-out that is not coming.

The dividend is not at risk and is not the reason people own this. At EUR 0.38 per share it costs about EUR 55 million against EUR 263 million of statutory free cash flow, a coverage ratio near five times, and yields only 2.4% - too low to have attracted a yield-focused shareholder base that could be forced out by a cut. There is no pivot to punish and no distribution to withdraw.

The flow that exists runs the other way. The EUR 100 million buyback is a persistent mechanical BID, not an offer: treasury stock rose from EUR 38 million at August 2025 to EUR 99 million at February 2026, so roughly EUR 61 million was executed in the half and the balance continues. On a EUR 2.14 billion market value that is a small but steady support.

The washout already happened and it was bought. The shares traded down to EUR 9.905 in the past 52 weeks on the Brazilian reform and have since recovered 57%, with the decisive turn coming on the 3 July 2026 third-quarter release when the shares rose about 6% on a revenue decline that was less severe than feared. That is the capitulation-and-recovery sequence completing, not beginning. The 50-day average of EUR 13.23 sits well below the 200-day of EUR 12.22 being crossed from beneath - momentum has turned positive, which is precisely why no forced seller remains.

One genuine overhang deserves naming: this is a 2024 spin-off from Sodexo, and spin-off shareholder bases turn over for years as index and mandate mismatches resolve. But that is a slow bleed, not a dated event, and after two years it is largely complete. There is no lock-up, no index deletion and no distressed holder to wait for.
moderator_conclusion:
Pass for now. This is a good business at a fair price, mis-screened as a great business at a free price, and the gap between those two readings is the entire finding.

What is genuinely true: Pluxee runs a 37% recurring EBITDA margin that expanded 229 basis points organically in the first half of fiscal 2026, converts 86% of it to cash, spends only 7.6% of revenue on capital, carries no net financial debt where its closest peer carries EUR 1.66 billion, and was affirmed BBB+ with a stable outlook by S&P Global Ratings on 7 July 2026. Its customer franchise is intact - business volume issued grew 9.4% organically in the third quarter while revenue fell 3.3%, which is exactly the signature of a company losing price rather than customers. Management pre-announced its own bad news in April before it appeared in a print, which is the behaviour of an honest board.

What is not true is the number that makes this look extraordinary. The file asserts EUR 2.02 billion of net cash against a EUR 2.14 billion market value. The company's own disclosure is EUR 1,270 million of net financial cash EXCLUDING restricted cash, and even that sits against EUR 4,076 million of vouchers owed to merchants and clients, with working capital of EUR 191 million and a current ratio of 1.04. The chief financial officer volunteered the distinction himself and disclosed that genuinely surplus cash FELL about EUR 140 million in the half. Roughly EUR 300 million is honestly available for a sum-of-the-parts, and the interest that float earns - about EUR 168 million a year, 13% of revenue - is already inside the EBITDA being capitalised, so counting the cash as well would value one asset twice. Separately, trailing diluted earnings per share is EUR 1.42, not the EUR 2.53 in the input, which nearly doubles the true price-to-earnings multiple to about 11 times.

Corrected, the picture is ordinary. Base-case fair value is EUR 18.00, roughly 13% above the EUR 15.60 close - a real discount, but far short of the 20% minimum this book requires for a new entry in the current risk-on, goldilocks regime, and the current regime read explicitly calls for WIDER entry discounts, not narrower, with sentiment gauges at their most complacent since 2021. The adverse case of EUR 12.50 is further away than the fair value is, so the asymmetry points the wrong way. Consensus across 14 analysts is about EUR 16.60 with a neutral rating; the shares have already run 57% off their low, sit 27% above the 200-day average and have effectively reached that target. On free cash flow yield - the one comparison the float cannot distort - Pluxee at 12.3% is marginally MORE expensive than Edenred at 12.9%.

The regime read cuts both ways and nets to neutral. It favours self-funding cash generators over capital burners, and Pluxee is emphatically the former. But it also demands resolution-driver independence, and this thesis rests on the same unresolved Brazilian regulatory factor that drives Edenred - the peer file is right that this is sector beta, not single-name alpha. Owning Pluxee alongside any other regulated- payments name is one bet wearing two tickets.

The moat judgement is what caps this. The closed two-sided network behind a tax-advantaged benefit was a genuine franchise, and it produced 50 basis points of take-rate expansion over four years - almost entirely from price. Brazil has now capped the merchant discount at 3.6% and, from 11 May 2026, forced migration to an open loop with a 2% regulated interchange, which dissolves the network itself in that market. Return on invested capital of 10.6% to 13.0% is respectable rather than fortress-grade, and gross margin is contracting. That is an eroding moat by the evidence, not a wide one, and the structural force is payments disintermediation - proprietary benefit rails giving way to open, regulated, general-purpose ones. It is material rather than terminal, because legislators are capping the take rate, not abolishing the benefit; volume still grows 9.4%. But an eroding moat caps the value score at 3, and on the evidence here that cap is deserved rather than merely applied.

What would change this. A close below roughly EUR 13.00 - the 50-day average - on a fiscal 2027 guidance disappointment at the 29 October 2026 results would restore a 25%-plus discount to fair value and make this a genuine entry. Alternatively, a buyback several times larger than the current EUR 100 million would prove the balance sheet holds real distributable value and would lift the fair value directly. Neither is in hand today. The catalyst is spent, the discount is thin, the peer gap is shared beta, and the price has already done most of the work.
sop_breakdown:

1. Continental Europe plus Rest of World employee benefits - about EUR 250 million of EBITDA at 6.3 times = EUR 1,575 million. The clean, unimpaired core: 5.1% organic growth in Continental Europe and 16.8% in Rest of World in the first half, 100% client retention.
2. Latin America - about EUR 84 million of EBITDA at 3.0 times = EUR 252 million. A deep discount to the peer multiple for the open-loop migration, with earnings still falling into fiscal 2027.
3. Float interest income - about EUR 150 million of EBITDA at 2.6 times = EUR 390 million. Low multiple deliberately: this is interest on other people's money, it is rate-dependent, and capitalising it is the alternative to adding the float cash, never a supplement to it.
Enterprise value EUR 2,217 million, plus EUR 300 million of genuinely surplus cash = equity EUR 2,517 million, or EUR 18.0 per share.

Two independent cross-checks, both of which are float-neutral and therefore more trustworthy than the enterprise-value build. On earnings: EUR 18.00 is 12.7 times trailing diluted earnings per share of EUR 1.42, a 10% discount to Edenred's 14.1 times, which is the right shape given Pluxee's revenue is falling 3.3% while the peer grows, offset by Pluxee carrying no net debt where Edenred carries EUR 1.66 billion. Both cross-checks land within a euro of the parts build.

Note the two corrections carried through this whole valuation: trailing diluted earnings per share is EUR 1.42, not the EUR 2.53 in the screening input; and net cash usable in a sum-of-the-parts is roughly EUR 300 million, not the EUR 2,020 million asserted there. risk_reward: Unfavourable at EUR 15.60. Upside to the base-case fair value of EUR 18.00 is EUR 2.40 per share; downside to the adverse case of EUR 12.50 is EUR 3.10 per share. interrogator_dossier:
# Forensic Dossier — Pluxee N.V. (PLX.PA)

**Prepared:** 2026-08-24 · **Listing:** Euronext Paris, quoted in euros · **Price used:** EUR 15.60 (last close, verified live)
**Transcripts reviewed:** Fiscal 2025 full-year call (2025-10-30) and First Half Fiscal 2026 call (2026-04-16)
**Post-transcript events verified independently:** Q3 Fiscal 2026 release (2026-07-03) and the S&P Global Ratings affirmation (2026-07-07)

Pluxee is the employee-benefits business spun out of Sodexo in 2024. It issues meal and lifestyle vouchers — increasingly digital cards and an app — that employers buy for their staff, and it earns money three ways: a fee from the employer client, a discount taken from the merchant who accepts the voucher, and interest on the large pool of cash it holds between the moment the employer pays and the moment the merchant is reimbursed. That cash pool is called the float, and it matters enormously to how this company should be valued.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

**The story compressed from "growth compounder" to "margin and cash compounder" in the space of two calls, and the compression was involuntary.**

At the fiscal 2025 results call in October 2025, the framing was expansion on every axis. Management led with "another very strong year, in which we executed our strategy with discipline and delivered above expectations across all key metrics," and the supporting facts were genuinely broad: 10.6% organic revenue growth, EUR 1.5 billion of annualised new client business against a EUR 1.3 billion target, and a free cash flow engine described as having gone "from circa EUR 290 million in fiscal 2023 to EUR 417 million in fiscal 2025." Even then, though, two things were quietly conceded: portfolio growth was "weaker... reflecting current macro uncertainties," and net retention had slipped to exactly 100% — the floor of the medium-term objective, not a cushion above it.

By the first-half fiscal 2026 call in April 2026, the top line had halved its pace. Total revenue grew 5.6% organically, down from 10.6%. The emphasis shifted decisively to what still worked: recurring earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) up 12.9% organically, margin up 229 basis points to 37%, and cash conversion at 86%. The sentence that best captures the new story is management's own: "EBITDA growing at twice the pace of top line growth." That is a perfectly respectable thing for a business to say — but it is a different thesis from the one sold six months earlier.

Three growth drivers were introduced or amplified across the two calls: face-value increases (legal caps on voucher values rising across several European countries), cross-selling beyond the core meal voucher, and bolt-on acquisitions (Cobee, Beneficio Facil, Skipr, ProEves). Two were quietly demoted: end-user portfolio growth, which management admitted "turned negative" in the second half of fiscal 2025, and public-benefit programmes, where governments in Romania and Austria suspended or reduced schemes "because of some budget constraints."

The decisive turn is not in either transcript. On 2026-07-03 Pluxee reported third-quarter revenue **down 3.3% organically**, with operating revenue down 4.1% and Latin America down 5.6%, and the full-year fiscal 2026 objective had by then been cut from high-single-digit organic revenue growth to **stable revenue**, and from roughly 100 basis points of margin expansion to **slight** expansion. The cause is Brazil's reform of the PAT meal-benefit programme: a 3.6% cap on the discount Pluxee may charge merchants, effective 2026-02-10, followed by migration to an open-loop card arrangement with a regulated 2% interchange fee from 2026-05-11. Management has told the market that the fourth quarter will carry roughly **twice** the third quarter's organic impact.

So the arc is: a confident spin-off compounder, then a margin-and-cash story, then a regulated utility fight in its second-largest region. The narrative did not shift because management changed its mind. It shifted because a regulator changed the rules.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

I tested management's five biggest claims against the reported numbers. Two important claims in the screener input I was handed turned out to be wrong, and I have corrected both.

| Management claim | Quarter | The evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Robust margin expansion... underscoring the operating leverage of our model" | FY25 and H1 FY26 | Trailing-twelve-month EBITDA of EUR 484 million on EUR 1,307 million of revenue is a 37.0% margin, versus 33.9% two years earlier. First-half margin expansion of 229 basis points is real and audited. | **Confirmed.** The strongest claim management makes. |
| "Outstanding cash generation and conversion" — 89% in FY25, 86% in H1 FY26 | FY25, H1 FY26 | True on the company's own "recurring free cash flow" definition (EUR 417 million in FY25, EUR 210 million in H1 FY26). But that definition includes the working-capital inflow generated by a growing float. On a statutory basis — operating cash flow of EUR 362 million less EUR 99 million of capital spending — trailing free cash flow is **EUR 263 million**, about 37% lower. | **Confirmed but flattered.** Both numbers are honest; they measure different things. The EUR 417 million figure borrows from a liability. |
| "Our free cash flow engine has expanded very materially" | FY25 | Statutory free cash flow: EUR 322 million (FY24) to EUR 311 million (FY25) to EUR 263 million (trailing to February 2026). The engine expanded on the company's measure and **contracted** on the statutory one. | **Diverges.** The story is richer than the audited cash flow statement justifies. |
| "We successfully managed to almost entirely absorb the regulatory change impact on merchant commissions" (Italy) | FY25 | Credible for Italy, and it is the single best piece of evidence for the bull case on Brazil. But the Brazilian reform is structurally harsher: Italy was a commission renegotiation; Brazil mandates migration to an **open loop**, which removes Pluxee's ability to set merchant economics at all. | **Confirmed for Italy; not transferable to Brazil.** |
| "Take-up rate improved 50 basis points over four years, vast majority from client commission" | FY25 | Consistent with the margin record. But it establishes that the earnings growth has come from **price**, not volume — and price is exactly what regulators are now capping. | **Confirmed, and it is a warning, not a comfort.** |

**Two corrections to the screener input, both material.**

First, the input asserts trailing diluted earnings per share of 2.53. The actual trailing figure to 2026-02-28 is **EUR 1.42** (net income of EUR 205 million on 144.5 million diluted shares). The 2.53 figure appears nowhere in the accounts and would understate the price-to-earnings multiple by roughly 44%.

Second — and this is the single most consequential number in the file — the input carries a "live correction" asserting **net cash of EUR 2.02 billion** as "a genuine sum-of-the-parts add-back." That figure is cash and short-term investments of EUR 3,313 million less total debt of EUR 1,293 million. It is arithmetically correct and economically wrong, for two reasons. It ignores roughly EUR 750 million of restricted cash — the company's own disclosed net financial cash position excluding restricted cash is **EUR 1,270 million** at 2026-02-28, not EUR 2.02 billion. And even that EUR 1,270 million is overwhelmingly float: it sits against **EUR 4,076 million of other current liabilities**, the money owed to merchants and clients for vouchers issued but not yet redeemed. Working capital is EUR 191 million and the current ratio is 1.04. This is not a company sitting on a spare EUR 2 billion.

The chief financial officer made the distinction himself in April 2026, and it is the most important thing he said all year: he separated the "overall net cash position" from "what we call this net excess cash position, making a clear distinction between the contribution of float related cash... and this excess cash," and disclosed that **excess cash fell by about EUR 140 million in the first half** while the float-related position improved by EUR 240 million. Management does not treat the float as distributable. Neither should we.

The low Altman-Z solvency score of 1.0 in the screener is, as suspected, an artefact of this float-heavy balance sheet rather than a distress signal — S&P Global Ratings affirmed **BBB+/A-2 with a stable outlook on 2026-07-07**. Equally, the reported return on equity of 68% is an artefact of a EUR 393 million equity base, not evidence of an exceptional franchise; return on invested capital of 10.6% to 13.0% is the honest measure, and it is good rather than great.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Declining, and specifically declining on revenue while holding firm on margin.**

*October 2025 — offensive.* The language is expansionary and unqualified: "delivered above expectations across all key metrics," "we are clearly well ahead of our initial plan," "a step change in the group's financial profile." Management volunteered a EUR 100 million buyback and framed it as conviction: "we are aware of where the stock price is currently trading, and versus the value we consider we are able to create from this company."

*April 2026 — defensive on the top line, offensive on costs.* The hedges arrive in the opening remarks: "amid a more uncertain macro and geopolitical environment," "even if other products and services is facing temporary pressure in specific activities." The confident material has migrated entirely to the cost line — "structural cost efficiency," "accelerated automation, notably through the increasing use of AI as a key optimization enabler," "a clear prioritization of projects." When pushed by UBS on whether the reiterated EBITDA guide was conservative, the chief financial officer refused the easy answer and instead volunteered bad news: Brazil "will weigh a lot on the EBITDA margin of the group... in the second half of the year, we will face a lower EBITDA margin compared to the previous year."

That last exchange is the most creditable moment in either transcript. Management had an open invitation to sandbag and declined it.

The clearest tonal tell is the answer to UBS on why clients are shrinking their headcount. Asked directly whether the end-user decline was driven by artificial-intelligence-related hiring freezes, the chief executive did not deny it — he named the exposed sectors: "the automotive industry, the IT industry and part of the interim industry are currently under pressure." Pluxee's revenue is a function of how many employees its clients have. That is a demand channel management has now acknowledged it cannot control.

**Trajectory: Declining on growth confidence, Stable-to-Rising on operational confidence.**

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Medium-High. Management has consistently delivered or beaten what it controls, and has been early and honest about what it does not.**

The delivery record on internal targets is genuinely strong. Fiscal 2025 promised low-double-digit organic growth and delivered 10.6%. It promised roughly 150 basis points of margin expansion and delivered 230. It promised cash conversion above 75% on average and delivered 89%. New client development targeted EUR 1.3 billion and delivered EUR 1.5 billion. Each of these was checkable and each was met.

The failure is on the revenue guide, and it is large: fiscal 2026 went from high-single-digit organic revenue growth to **stable**. That is not a rounding error. But the cause is a sovereign regulator, it was flagged to investors at the half-year before it appeared in the numbers, and the fourth-quarter magnitude was pre-announced at roughly twice the third quarter's. Management did not let the market discover this.

Set against that, the screener records an earnings beat rate of **2 of 6 quarters (33%)** and consensus forward earnings growth of just **+0.3%**. The market has already stopped extrapolating.

There is one soft spot worth flagging. Management repeatedly guides to cash conversion "over 80% on average" and then stresses the word *over* — "we are not guiding on an 80% achievement, we are guiding on over 80%." That is a target constructed to be difficult to miss, on a metric that includes the float working-capital inflow. It is the one place where the disclosure is engineered rather than plain.

**Reliability: Medium-High.** High on margin, cost and cash. Medium on revenue, because the revenue is partly in the gift of legislators.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Four themes recur, and management engages seriously with three of them.

**The cash pile — pressed twice, answered evasively both times.** Deutsche Bank's Andre Juillard asked directly in April 2026: "Your cash net position is even stronger than what it was at the end of last year. Do you have any new plan about the use of this cash or still not clear?" The answer was that mergers and acquisitions remain "a key pillar," that the pipeline is "solid," and "we'll come back to you when it will be." In October 2025, the same analyst summarised the buyback answer as "the message is step by step," to which the chief financial officer replied "as always." Analysts are asking the exact right question — if the balance sheet is as strong as claimed, why is the return so small? — and are being deferred.

**Cross-selling — asked for numbers, given a direction.** Bernstein's Sabrina Blanc asked twice for the weight of non-meal-voucher solutions in operating revenue. She received: "the contribution coming from the cross-selling in percentage is higher than the overall growth." That is a ratio, not a level. Cross-selling is load-bearing in the medium-term story and remains unquantified.

**Cash conversion sustainability — pressed by Barclays, answered candidly.** Pravin Gondhale asked whether 90% conversion could persist. The chief financial officer explained that working capital swings with business growth and regulation, which is the honest answer and implicitly concedes the float dependency.

**Client headcount and artificial intelligence — raised by UBS, answered but not resolved.** This is the topic analysts pushed on that management is least able to address, because it is a second-order exposure: Pluxee does not lose clients, its clients lose employees. Net retention has already fallen to exactly 100% on this mechanism.

The topic no analyst pushed hard enough on, in either call, is what the Brazilian open-loop migration does to the structure of the business rather than to one year's revenue. That is the question that matters most and it went largely unasked.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **The Brazilian reform attacks the business model, not just the margin.** A 3.6% cap on the merchant discount rate compresses price. Migration to an open loop with a 2% regulated interchange fee from 2026-05-11 removes the closed network itself — the thing that made this a franchise rather than a card programme.

🔴 **Growth has come from price, and price is now regulated.** Management's own disclosure: 50 basis points of take-rate improvement over four years, "the vast majority... coming from the increase in the client commission." Volume growth, meanwhile, is negative at the end-user level.

🔴 **Net retention is at the floor, not above it.** 100% in fiscal 2025 and only "resilient" in the first half of fiscal 2026, with the end-user portfolio contribution having "turned negative" in the second half of fiscal 2025.

🔴 **Public-benefit programmes are a sovereign-budget derivative.** Romania and Austria suspended or reduced schemes "because of some budget constraints." This revenue line is exposed to European fiscal consolidation.

🔴 **The statutory cash flow is materially below the headline.** EUR 263 million trailing versus EUR 417 million on the company measure.

🔴 **Buyback is token relative to the claimed balance-sheet strength.** EUR 100 million against a EUR 2.14 billion market value — 4.7% — while management defers capital-return questions in favour of an unspecified acquisition pipeline.

🟢 **Margin execution is excellent and repeatable.** 229–268 basis points of organic expansion in the first half of fiscal 2026, on top of 230 in fiscal 2025, driven by a single platform architecture with genuine operating leverage.

🟢 **Business volume is still growing strongly even as revenue falls.** Third-quarter volume issued rose 9.4% organically to EUR 6.6 billion while revenue fell 3.3%. The customer franchise is intact; the price per unit is what regulation took.

🟢 **Investment-grade and unlevered.** S&P affirmed BBB+/A-2, stable, on 2026-07-07. Unlike its closest peer, Pluxee carries no net financial debt.

🟢 **Management pre-announced its own bad news.** The Brazil second-half margin hit was disclosed in April, before it appeared in any print.

🟢 **The third quarter landed better than feared** — the shares rose about 6% on the 2026-07-03 release, and the nine-month revenue figure still showed 2.7% organic growth.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**"Payment agnostic" is the tell.** In October 2025 management described the app's key strength as "being fully payment agnostic, it integrates the most popular digital payment options such as Google Pay, Apple Pay, and QR code solutions." That is presented as a feature. Read structurally, it is an admission that the proprietary payment rail — the closed loop — is no longer where the value sits. Brazil's regulator has now mandated exactly that outcome.

**The vocabulary migrated from acquisition to efficiency.** In October 2025 the recurring words are "new client development," "cross-selling," "face value." By April 2026 they are "operating leverage," "streamlining," "automation," "rigorous value creation monitoring." Artificial intelligence appears in both calls but in opposite roles: in October it is a customer-facing innovation ("AI-powered chatbots"); in April it is a cost lever ("a key optimization enabler") *and* a threat to clients' headcount. The same technology moved from the growth column to the cost column to the risk column in six months.

**"We are always very selective in this kind of program" is retrospective justification.** Applied to public benefits after governments cut them, it reframes a lost contract cycle as portfolio discipline.

**The United Kingdom and United States exit is being pre-buried.** Described as "strategically refocusing" and "progressively exiting noncore, lower return activities," with the reassurance that they "account for less than 5% of group revenues" and "should return to a positive contribution from fiscal 2027." Two years after a spin-off, two developed markets are being wound back.

**The chief financial officer's float-versus-excess-cash disaggregation was unprompted.** He volunteered a distinction that makes the balance sheet look weaker. That is a mark of integrity — and it is also the single fact that dismantles the "EUR 2 billion of net cash" version of this investment case.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: PIVOTING.**

This is not a deteriorating business and it is not a compounder either. It is a well-run franchise executing a genuine pivot — from volume-and-price growth to efficiency and cash conversion — forced on it by regulators in its most profitable region. The operational execution is real: 37% EBITDA margins, 86% cash conversion, investment-grade and unlevered, and business volume still compounding at 9.4% while revenue falls.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: the balance sheet is not what the screening file says it is.** The investment case for Pluxee rests almost entirely on whether roughly EUR 1.27 billion of net financial cash — against a EUR 2.14 billion market value — is shareholders' money or merchants' money. The company's own chief financial officer says most of it is float, and the company's own behaviour agrees: a EUR 55 million dividend and a EUR 100 million buyback are what management believes it can safely return. Anyone underwriting this at "trades below net cash" is underwriting a number the company does not recognise. Size to an enterprise value that credits perhaps EUR 250–350 million of genuinely surplus cash, not EUR 2 billion.

**Economic moat: a regulatory-licence and two-sided-network moat, ERODING.**

The moat type is real and identifiable: a tax-advantaged benefit mandated or incentivised by governments, delivered through a closed two-sided network of employers and merchants where both sides face switching costs. It produced a near-duopoly with Edenred and a take rate management could push up 50 basis points over four years.

The width evidence says erosion, not strength. Return on invested capital is 10.6% to 13.0% — respectable, not fortress-grade. Gross margin is contracting. The take rate, the direct measure of pricing power, is now capped by statute in Brazil at 3.6% on the merchant side. Most decisively, the migration to an open loop with a regulated 2% interchange from 2026-05-11 dissolves the closed network in that market — it converts a proprietary rail into a card programme competing on general-purpose payment infrastructure. A high margin that is falling because a regulator capped the price is the textbook definition of an eroding moat, not a wide one.

**Secular threat: MATERIAL, not terminal — the force is payments disintermediation.**

The structural force is the replacement of proprietary closed-loop benefit networks by open, regulated, general-purpose payment rails with capped interchange. Brazil has done it. The European Union's broader direction on instant payments and interchange caps points the same way, and Italy, France and Romania have each already touched voucher economics.

It is material rather than terminal for one specific reason: the underlying *demand* is a tax-advantaged employee benefit created by legislation, and no regulator has moved to abolish the benefit itself. Employers still want it, employees still receive it, and volume is still growing at 9.4%. What is being taken is the take rate, not the market. Pluxee will still be here in ten years; the question is whether it earns 37% EBITDA margins or 25%.

**Cheapness: partly a fear print, partly a shrinking base — and mostly already recovered.** At EUR 15.60 the shares trade at about 11 times trailing earnings on a roughly 12% free cash flow yield, against a closest peer at about 14 times. That is a real but modest discount, and it is a discount driven by a shared regulatory shock that hit both companies — sector beta, not a mispricing unique to Pluxee. Critically, the fear print has largely been paid: the shares are 57% above their 52-week low of EUR 9.905, 27% above their 200-day average, and sit essentially **on top of the analyst consensus target of about EUR 16.60**. The washed-out price was available in the spring. It is not available now.

Management credibility 3 of 5 · trajectory turning · a moat that is being eroded · moat trend eroding · structural threat material.

bull_thesis:
Pluxee is the employee-benefits business spun out of Sodexo in 2024. Employers buy meal and lifestyle vouchers for their staff; Pluxee earns a fee from the employer, a discount from the merchant who accepts the voucher, and interest on the cash it holds between the two. The bullish case rests on four things that are verifiably true today.

First, the operating machine is excellent and improving. Recurring earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) margin reached 37% in the first half of fiscal 2026, up 229 basis points organically, on top of 230 basis points in fiscal 2025. Trailing-twelve-month EBITDA to 28 February 2026 was EUR 484 million on EUR 1,307 million of revenue. Cash conversion ran at 86% in the half and 89% the year before, against a target of above 75%. Management credits a single shared platform and heavy automation, and the numbers corroborate the claim rather than merely decorating it.

Second, the customer franchise is intact even though revenue fell. In the third quarter reported on 3 July 2026, business volume issued rose 9.4% organically to EUR 6.6 billion while revenue fell 3.3%. That gap is the whole argument: Pluxee is not losing clients or volume, it is being denied price by a regulator in one country. New client wins hit a record EUR 0.9 billion of annualised volume in the first half, with small and medium enterprises above 30% of new business, and client retention held at 100%.

Third, the balance sheet is genuinely unlevered in a sector where the peer is not. Pluxee reported net financial cash excluding restricted cash of EUR 1,270 million at 28 February 2026, up from EUR 1,163 million at 31 August 2025, and S&P Global Ratings affirmed BBB+/A-2 with a stable outlook on 7 July 2026. Its closest comparable, Edenred, carries roughly EUR 1.66 billion of net debt. Even crediting only the genuinely surplus slice of that cash, Pluxee holds capacity it is not using, and management has begun to use it: a EUR 0.38 dividend and a EUR 100 million buyback, of which roughly EUR 61 million had been executed by February.

Fourth, there is a live precedent for absorbing exactly this shock. Italy capped merchant commissions and management told the October 2025 call it had 'almost entirely absorbed' the impact by renegotiating client pricing. If Brazil follows the Italian path, the fiscal 2026 revenue reset is a one-off reset of the base rather than a permanent impairment, and fiscal 2027 recovers as the United Kingdom and United States refocus turns positive, European legal caps on voucher face values flow through, and the comparison base normalises. On that path the shares earn something close to the peer multiple of about 14 times earnings on a recovered EUR 1.65 to 1.70 of earnings per share, which is the bull number.
bear_thesis:
The bearish case is not that Pluxee is a bad business. It is that the thing being taken from it is permanent, that the balance sheet is far weaker than the screen suggests, and that the discount has already been paid.

Start with the balance sheet, because it is where this file is most wrong. The screening input asserts EUR 2.02 billion of net cash as 'a genuine sum-of-the-parts add-back' against a EUR 2.14 billion market value. That figure ignores roughly EUR 750 million of restricted cash and, more importantly, ignores what the cash is for. It sits against EUR 4,076 million of other current liabilities, the money owed to merchants and clients for vouchers issued but not yet redeemed. Working capital is EUR 191 million and the current ratio is 1.04. The chief financial officer drew the distinction himself in April 2026, separating the 'overall net cash position' from the 'net excess cash position', and disclosed that excess cash actually fell about EUR 140 million in the first half while the float-related position rose EUR 240 million. Management does not treat this money as distributable, and its own capital returns of EUR 155 million in total confirm it. Any thesis of the form 'it trades below net cash' is underwriting a number the company does not recognise.

There is a second, subtler trap in that cash. Roughly EUR 168 million a year of Pluxee's revenue is interest earned on the float, about 13% of total revenue at close to a 100% margin. That income exists only because the float cash exists. An investor who both capitalises the interest income inside EBITDA and adds the float cash as net cash has counted the same asset twice. Worse, that income is a rate annuity, not a franchise, and it shrinks as European rates ease.

Now the operating impairment. Brazil capped the merchant discount rate at 3.6% effective 10 February 2026 and, from 11 May 2026, mandated migration to an open-loop card arrangement with a regulated 2% interchange fee. The first cap compresses price; the second dissolves the closed two-sided network that made this a franchise at all, turning a proprietary rail into a card programme competing on general-purpose payment infrastructure. This is structurally harsher than Italy, where the fix was a commission renegotiation inside a network Pluxee still controlled. Third-quarter Latin American operating revenue fell 5.6% organically, management guided the fourth quarter to roughly twice that impact, and has flagged continued pressure into early fiscal 2027. Fiscal 2026 guidance was cut from high-single-digit organic revenue growth to stable, and from about 100 basis points of margin expansion to slight.

Underneath that sits a demand problem management cannot control. Asked by UBS in April whether clients were shrinking headcount because of artificial intelligence, the chief executive named the exposed sectors: automotive, information technology and staffing. Pluxee's revenue is a function of how many employees its clients have, and net retention has already fallen to exactly 100% on this mechanism, with end-user portfolio contribution having 'turned negative' in the second half of fiscal 2025. Growth over four years came from a 50 basis point rise in take rate, 'the vast majority... coming from the increase in the client commission' - that is, from price. Price is what is now capped.

Finally, the entry point. At EUR 15.60 the shares are 57% above their 52-week low of EUR 9.905, 27% above their 200-day average, and sit essentially on top of the analyst consensus target of about EUR 16.60 (14 analysts, neutral consensus, 3 buy / 9 hold / 2 sell). On trailing earnings of EUR 1.42 the shares trade at about 11 times, against Edenred at about 14 times - a real but modest gap that is explained by Brazil concentration, not by mispricing. On free cash flow yield the two are indistinguishable: 12.3% for Pluxee versus 12.9% for Edenred. The washed-out price was available in the spring. What is left is a fair price for a good business whose moat is being narrowed by statute.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market is not the direction - it is the balance sheet, and our disagreement cuts AGAINST the bullish reading rather than for it.

The street assumption that is wrong is not a sell-side one; it is the one embedded in the screening file and in most quantitative treatments of this name: that Pluxee holds EUR 2.02 billion of net cash against a EUR 2.14 billion market value, and therefore that the operating business is nearly free. That is the single most seductive number on this file and it does not survive contact with the accounts. It ignores roughly EUR 750 million of restricted cash - the company's own disclosed net financial cash excluding restricted cash is EUR 1,270 million at 28 February 2026 - and it ignores the EUR 4,076 million of other current liabilities the cash exists to settle. Working capital is EUR 191 million; the current ratio is 1.04. The chief financial officer separated 'overall net cash' from 'net excess cash' unprompted on the April 2026 call and disclosed that excess cash FELL about EUR 140 million in the half. Management's own capital returns - EUR 55 million of dividend and a EUR 100 million buyback, together 7% of market value - are the honest revealed estimate of what is actually surplus.

There is a related double-count that anyone building an enterprise value here should be alert to. About EUR 168 million a year, roughly 13% of revenue at close to a 100% margin, is interest earned on the float. Capitalise that income inside EBITDA and you have valued the float. Add the float cash as net cash as well and you have valued the same asset twice. Our valuation does the first and refuses the second.

Two lesser but material corrections. The screening input's trailing diluted earnings per share of EUR 2.53 is wrong; the actual figure to 28 February 2026 is EUR 1.42, which raises the true price-to-earnings multiple from about 6 times to about 11 times. And the input's discounted cash flow fair value of EUR 72 and 'margin of safety 51%' are model artefacts built on those inputs; the published analyst consensus is about EUR 16.60 across 14 analysts with a neutral rating, which the shares have already reached.

Where the street may genuinely be too pessimistic is narrower and worth naming honestly: business volume issued still grew 9.4% organically in the third quarter while revenue fell 3.3%, which says the franchise is intact and only the price per unit was taken. If the Italian precedent repeats, fiscal 2027 is a base reset rather than an impairment. That is a real argument. It is worth perhaps EUR 2 to 3 per share, not the EUR 30 to 50 the screening file's arithmetic implies - and at EUR 15.60 the market has already paid most of it.
forcing_function:
The hard date is 29 October 2026: Pluxee reports full-year fiscal 2026 results, following the 30 October 2025 precedent for the prior year. This is the only dated event in the window that can force a re-rating in either direction, and it is worth being clear that it is more likely to force one DOWNWARD, because it carries the first quantified fiscal 2027 guidance against a stock already at its consensus target. A secondary date follows: the annual general meeting on 17 December 2026, which approves the dividend and is the natural venue for any enlarged buyback authorisation.

The event that would genuinely force an upward re-rating is not on the calendar, and that is the problem. It would be a decisive capital-allocation move - a buyback several times the current EUR 100 million, or a special distribution - that proved the balance sheet holds distributable value rather than merchants' float. Management has been asked twice, by Deutsche Bank in both October 2025 and April 2026, and has twice deferred, answering that mergers and acquisitions remain 'a key pillar', that the pipeline is 'solid', and 'we'll come back to you when it will be'. Until that changes, the cash stays a talking point rather than a catalyst, and the deferral is itself informative: management does not believe the money is as free as the screen thinks.

The regulatory clock offers no forcing function either. The Brazilian reform's dated milestones - the 3.6% cap on 10 February 2026 and the open-loop migration on 11 May 2026 - are both behind us. What remains is a slow accumulation of evidence about how much margin the open loop permanently costs, and that resolves over fiscal 2027 quarterly prints, not at a single moment.
valley_of_death:
The next three to nine months contain one scheduled hazard and one structural one, and neither is a cash crisis - this is a business with investment-grade credit, EUR 263 million of statutory trailing free cash flow, capital spending of only 7.6% of revenue and no maturity wall. The risk is to the multiple, not to solvency.

The scheduled hazard is the full-year fiscal 2026 results on 29 October 2026. Two things land that day. First, the fourth quarter, which management has pre-announced will carry roughly twice the third quarter's organic impact - implying roughly a 7% organic revenue decline in the quarter and a lower group EBITDA margin than the prior year, exactly as the chief financial officer warned in April. Second, and more dangerous, fiscal 2027 guidance. Management has so far said only that it expects 'continued pressure in early fiscal 2027'. That is an unquantified negative sitting in front of a stock that has already recovered 57% from its low and trades at its consensus target. A fiscal 2027 guide that implies flat or down earnings against the current EUR 1.42 base is the single most likely cause of a de-rating back toward the 50-day average of EUR 13.23 or below.

The structural hazard is that the Brazilian open-loop migration, live since 11 May 2026, has not yet been observed through a full annual cycle. The 3.6% merchant-discount cap is a price effect and is now measurable. The open-loop conversion is a structure effect - it removes Pluxee's control of merchant economics entirely - and its full margin consequence will only be visible in fiscal 2027 numbers. The Italian absorption precedent works by renegotiating client pricing inside a network you still control; that lever is weaker when the network is open.

Two smaller drags run alongside. The United Kingdom and United States businesses, together under 5% of revenue, will continue to weigh on growth through the second half of fiscal 2026 before management expects them to turn positive in fiscal 2027. And float interest income, roughly EUR 168 million annually at near 100% margin, is a rate annuity: any European easing cycle compresses it directly, and no operational improvement offsets it.
positioning_washout:
There is no mechanical forced-selling dynamic available here, and this is the part of the setup that most clearly argues against waiting for a wash-out that is not coming.

The dividend is not at risk and is not the reason people own this. At EUR 0.38 per share it costs about EUR 55 million against EUR 263 million of statutory free cash flow, a coverage ratio near five times, and yields only 2.4% - too low to have attracted a yield-focused shareholder base that could be forced out by a cut. There is no pivot to punish and no distribution to withdraw.

The flow that exists runs the other way. The EUR 100 million buyback is a persistent mechanical BID, not an offer: treasury stock rose from EUR 38 million at August 2025 to EUR 99 million at February 2026, so roughly EUR 61 million was executed in the half and the balance continues. On a EUR 2.14 billion market value that is a small but steady support.

The washout already happened and it was bought. The shares traded down to EUR 9.905 in the past 52 weeks on the Brazilian reform and have since recovered 57%, with the decisive turn coming on the 3 July 2026 third-quarter release when the shares rose about 6% on a revenue decline that was less severe than feared. That is the capitulation-and-recovery sequence completing, not beginning. The 50-day average of EUR 13.23 sits well below the 200-day of EUR 12.22 being crossed from beneath - momentum has turned positive, which is precisely why no forced seller remains.

One genuine overhang deserves naming: this is a 2024 spin-off from Sodexo, and spin-off shareholder bases turn over for years as index and mandate mismatches resolve. But that is a slow bleed, not a dated event, and after two years it is largely complete. There is no lock-up, no index deletion and no distressed holder to wait for.
moderator_conclusion:
Pass for now. This is a good business at a fair price, mis-screened as a great business at a free price, and the gap between those two readings is the entire finding.

What is genuinely true: Pluxee runs a 37% recurring EBITDA margin that expanded 229 basis points organically in the first half of fiscal 2026, converts 86% of it to cash, spends only 7.6% of revenue on capital, carries no net financial debt where its closest peer carries EUR 1.66 billion, and was affirmed BBB+ with a stable outlook by S&P Global Ratings on 7 July 2026. Its customer franchise is intact - business volume issued grew 9.4% organically in the third quarter while revenue fell 3.3%, which is exactly the signature of a company losing price rather than customers. Management pre-announced its own bad news in April before it appeared in a print, which is the behaviour of an honest board.

What is not true is the number that makes this look extraordinary. The file asserts EUR 2.02 billion of net cash against a EUR 2.14 billion market value. The company's own disclosure is EUR 1,270 million of net financial cash EXCLUDING restricted cash, and even that sits against EUR 4,076 million of vouchers owed to merchants and clients, with working capital of EUR 191 million and a current ratio of 1.04. The chief financial officer volunteered the distinction himself and disclosed that genuinely surplus cash FELL about EUR 140 million in the half. Roughly EUR 300 million is honestly available for a sum-of-the-parts, and the interest that float earns - about EUR 168 million a year, 13% of revenue - is already inside the EBITDA being capitalised, so counting the cash as well would value one asset twice. Separately, trailing diluted earnings per share is EUR 1.42, not the EUR 2.53 in the input, which nearly doubles the true price-to-earnings multiple to about 11 times.

Corrected, the picture is ordinary. Base-case fair value is EUR 18.00, roughly 13% above the EUR 15.60 close - a real discount, but far short of the 20% minimum this book requires for a new entry in the current risk-on, goldilocks regime, and the current regime read explicitly calls for WIDER entry discounts, not narrower, with sentiment gauges at their most complacent since 2021. The adverse case of EUR 12.50 is further away than the fair value is, so the asymmetry points the wrong way. Consensus across 14 analysts is about EUR 16.60 with a neutral rating; the shares have already run 57% off their low, sit 27% above the 200-day average and have effectively reached that target. On free cash flow yield - the one comparison the float cannot distort - Pluxee at 12.3% is marginally MORE expensive than Edenred at 12.9%.

The regime read cuts both ways and nets to neutral. It favours self-funding cash generators over capital burners, and Pluxee is emphatically the former. But it also demands resolution-driver independence, and this thesis rests on the same unresolved Brazilian regulatory factor that drives Edenred - the peer file is right that this is sector beta, not single-name alpha. Owning Pluxee alongside any other regulated- payments name is one bet wearing two tickets.

The moat judgement is what caps this. The closed two-sided network behind a tax-advantaged benefit was a genuine franchise, and it produced 50 basis points of take-rate expansion over four years - almost entirely from price. Brazil has now capped the merchant discount at 3.6% and, from 11 May 2026, forced migration to an open loop with a 2% regulated interchange, which dissolves the network itself in that market. Return on invested capital of 10.6% to 13.0% is respectable rather than fortress-grade, and gross margin is contracting. That is an eroding moat by the evidence, not a wide one, and the structural force is payments disintermediation - proprietary benefit rails giving way to open, regulated, general-purpose ones. It is material rather than terminal, because legislators are capping the take rate, not abolishing the benefit; volume still grows 9.4%. But an eroding moat caps the value score at 3, and on the evidence here that cap is deserved rather than merely applied.

What would change this. A close below roughly EUR 13.00 - the 50-day average - on a fiscal 2027 guidance disappointment at the 29 October 2026 results would restore a 25%-plus discount to fair value and make this a genuine entry. Alternatively, a buyback several times larger than the current EUR 100 million would prove the balance sheet holds real distributable value and would lift the fair value directly. Neither is in hand today. The catalyst is spent, the discount is thin, the peer gap is shared beta, and the price has already done most of the work.
sop_breakdown:
Base case EUR 18.00 per share on roughly 140 million shares (147.45 million issued less about 7.6 million in treasury after the buyback). Parts:
1. Continental Europe plus Rest of World employee benefits - about EUR 250 million of EBITDA at 6.3 times = EUR 1,575 million. The clean, unimpaired core: 5.1% organic growth in Continental Europe and 16.8% in Rest of World in the first half, 100% client retention.
2. Latin America - about EUR 84 million of EBITDA at 3.0 times = EUR 252 million. A deep discount to the peer multiple for the open-loop migration, with earnings still falling into fiscal 2027.
3. Float interest income - about EUR 150 million of EBITDA at 2.6 times = EUR 390 million. Low multiple deliberately: this is interest on other people's money, it is rate-dependent, and capitalising it is the alternative to adding the float cash, never a supplement to it.
Enterprise value EUR 2,217 million, plus EUR 300 million of genuinely surplus cash = equity EUR 2,517 million, or EUR 18.0 per share.

Two independent cross-checks, both of which are float-neutral and therefore more trustworthy than the enterprise-value build. On earnings: EUR 18.00 is 12.7 times trailing diluted earnings per share of EUR 1.42, a 10% discount to Edenred's 14.1 times, which is the right shape given Pluxee's revenue is falling 3.3% while the peer grows, offset by Pluxee carrying no net debt where Edenred carries EUR 1.66 billion. On cash: EUR 18.00 implies a 10.4% free cash flow yield on statutory trailing free cash flow of EUR 263 million (operating cash flow EUR 362 million less EUR 99 million capital expenditure) - not the company's EUR 417 million 'recurring' measure, which includes the float working-capital inflow and is therefore partly borrowed. Both cross-checks land within a euro of the parts build.

Note the two corrections carried through this whole valuation: trailing diluted earnings per share is EUR 1.42, not the EUR 2.53 in the screening input; and net cash usable in a sum-of-the-parts is roughly EUR 300 million, not the EUR 2,020 million asserted there. Using the input's figures produces a fair value roughly double this one, entirely on arithmetic the company's own chief financial officer has publicly disowned.
risk_reward: Unfavourable at EUR 15.60. Upside to the base-case fair value of EUR 18.00 is EUR 2.40 per share; downside to the adverse case of EUR 12.50 is EUR 3.10 per share. The favourable case of EUR 24.00 sits above the highest published street target of EUR 22.90 and requires Brazil to be absorbed on the Italian precedent, which the open-loop mandate makes materially harder. There is no structural downside floor: no deal terms, no tender, and the balance sheet cash is float rather than shareholders' money, so it cannot be used as a backstop. The 2.4% dividend yield is not a floor either.
peer_comps_note:
The peer file flags this pairing as sector-regulatory convergence, and that call is correct and decisive: Pluxee and Edenred are the employee-benefits near-duopoly and both de-rated on the SAME unresolved driver - the Brazilian PAT reform plus the Italian voucher cap, with Kepler cutting both names on the one event. The gap between them is therefore shared-factor SECTOR BETA, not idiosyncratic single-name alpha, and I am explicitly NOT crediting it as name-specific edge. In a book that enforces resolution-driver independence, a Pluxee seat alongside any other regulated-payments name is one bet, not two.

One correction to the supplied anchor, made on live data rather than memory. The peer file carries Edenred at about 10.3 times forward earnings and 4.1 times forward enterprise value to EBITDA, sourced 'as of 2026-06'. Edenred has re-rated hard since: at EUR 29.94 on 22 August 2026 it is at its 52-week high (52-week low EUR 15.23), 44% above its 200-day average of EUR 20.78, and now trades at 14.1 times trailing earnings and 7.8 times trailing enterprise value to EBITDA. So the anchor is stale in the OPPOSITE direction from the one the file warned about - it understates the peer, which flatters Pluxee's apparent discount. I have used the live figures throughout.

On the live anchors: Pluxee at EUR 15.60 trades at 11.0 times trailing earnings against Edenred's 14.1 - a 22% discount, real but modest. On enterprise value to EBITDA the gap looks enormous (2.8 times versus 7.8 times) but that comparison is an artefact, not a signal: it is driven almost entirely by netting off Pluxee's float cash on one side while Edenred carries EUR 1.66 billion of genuine net debt on the other. The cleanest apples-to-apples read is free cash flow yield, which is float-neutral, and there the two are indistinguishable - 12.3% for Pluxee versus 12.9% for Edenred. On the metric that cannot be gamed by the balance sheet, Pluxee is marginally the more expensive of the two. Sodexo, the former parent, at EUR 57.00 is a different business (food services) and is not a valuation anchor here.
interrogator_dossier:
# Forensic Dossier — Pluxee N.V. (PLX.PA)

**Prepared:** 2026-08-24 · **Listing:** Euronext Paris, quoted in euros · **Price used:** EUR 15.60 (last close, verified live)
**Transcripts reviewed:** Fiscal 2025 full-year call (2025-10-30) and First Half Fiscal 2026 call (2026-04-16)
**Post-transcript events verified independently:** Q3 Fiscal 2026 release (2026-07-03) and the S&P Global Ratings affirmation (2026-07-07)

Pluxee is the employee-benefits business spun out of Sodexo in 2024. It issues meal and lifestyle vouchers — increasingly digital cards and an app — that employers buy for their staff, and it earns money three ways: a fee from the employer client, a discount taken from the merchant who accepts the voucher, and interest on the large pool of cash it holds between the moment the employer pays and the moment the merchant is reimbursed. That cash pool is called the float, and it matters enormously to how this company should be valued.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

**The story compressed from "growth compounder" to "margin and cash compounder" in the space of two calls, and the compression was involuntary.**

At the fiscal 2025 results call in October 2025, the framing was expansion on every axis. Management led with "another very strong year, in which we executed our strategy with discipline and delivered above expectations across all key metrics," and the supporting facts were genuinely broad: 10.6% organic revenue growth, EUR 1.5 billion of annualised new client business against a EUR 1.3 billion target, and a free cash flow engine described as having gone "from circa EUR 290 million in fiscal 2023 to EUR 417 million in fiscal 2025." Even then, though, two things were quietly conceded: portfolio growth was "weaker... reflecting current macro uncertainties," and net retention had slipped to exactly 100% — the floor of the medium-term objective, not a cushion above it.

By the first-half fiscal 2026 call in April 2026, the top line had halved its pace. Total revenue grew 5.6% organically, down from 10.6%. The emphasis shifted decisively to what still worked: recurring earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) up 12.9% organically, margin up 229 basis points to 37%, and cash conversion at 86%. The sentence that best captures the new story is management's own: "EBITDA growing at twice the pace of top line growth." That is a perfectly respectable thing for a business to say — but it is a different thesis from the one sold six months earlier.

Three growth drivers were introduced or amplified across the two calls: face-value increases (legal caps on voucher values rising across several European countries), cross-selling beyond the core meal voucher, and bolt-on acquisitions (Cobee, Beneficio Facil, Skipr, ProEves). Two were quietly demoted: end-user portfolio growth, which management admitted "turned negative" in the second half of fiscal 2025, and public-benefit programmes, where governments in Romania and Austria suspended or reduced schemes "because of some budget constraints."

The decisive turn is not in either transcript. On 2026-07-03 Pluxee reported third-quarter revenue **down 3.3% organically**, with operating revenue down 4.1% and Latin America down 5.6%, and the full-year fiscal 2026 objective had by then been cut from high-single-digit organic revenue growth to **stable revenue**, and from roughly 100 basis points of margin expansion to **slight** expansion. The cause is Brazil's reform of the PAT meal-benefit programme: a 3.6% cap on the discount Pluxee may charge merchants, effective 2026-02-10, followed by migration to an open-loop card arrangement with a regulated 2% interchange fee from 2026-05-11. Management has told the market that the fourth quarter will carry roughly **twice** the third quarter's organic impact.

So the arc is: a confident spin-off compounder, then a margin-and-cash story, then a regulated utility fight in its second-largest region. The narrative did not shift because management changed its mind. It shifted because a regulator changed the rules.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

I tested management's five biggest claims against the reported numbers. Two important claims in the screener input I was handed turned out to be wrong, and I have corrected both.

| Management claim | Quarter | The evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Robust margin expansion... underscoring the operating leverage of our model" | FY25 and H1 FY26 | Trailing-twelve-month EBITDA of EUR 484 million on EUR 1,307 million of revenue is a 37.0% margin, versus 33.9% two years earlier. First-half margin expansion of 229 basis points is real and audited. | **Confirmed.** The strongest claim management makes. |
| "Outstanding cash generation and conversion" — 89% in FY25, 86% in H1 FY26 | FY25, H1 FY26 | True on the company's own "recurring free cash flow" definition (EUR 417 million in FY25, EUR 210 million in H1 FY26). But that definition includes the working-capital inflow generated by a growing float. On a statutory basis — operating cash flow of EUR 362 million less EUR 99 million of capital spending — trailing free cash flow is **EUR 263 million**, about 37% lower. | **Confirmed but flattered.** Both numbers are honest; they measure different things. The EUR 417 million figure borrows from a liability. |
| "Our free cash flow engine has expanded very materially" | FY25 | Statutory free cash flow: EUR 322 million (FY24) to EUR 311 million (FY25) to EUR 263 million (trailing to February 2026). The engine expanded on the company's measure and **contracted** on the statutory one. | **Diverges.** The story is richer than the audited cash flow statement justifies. |
| "We successfully managed to almost entirely absorb the regulatory change impact on merchant commissions" (Italy) | FY25 | Credible for Italy, and it is the single best piece of evidence for the bull case on Brazil. But the Brazilian reform is structurally harsher: Italy was a commission renegotiation; Brazil mandates migration to an **open loop**, which removes Pluxee's ability to set merchant economics at all. | **Confirmed for Italy; not transferable to Brazil.** |
| "Take-up rate improved 50 basis points over four years, vast majority from client commission" | FY25 | Consistent with the margin record. But it establishes that the earnings growth has come from **price**, not volume — and price is exactly what regulators are now capping. | **Confirmed, and it is a warning, not a comfort.** |

**Two corrections to the screener input, both material.**

First, the input asserts trailing diluted earnings per share of 2.53. The actual trailing figure to 2026-02-28 is **EUR 1.42** (net income of EUR 205 million on 144.5 million diluted shares). The 2.53 figure appears nowhere in the accounts and would understate the price-to-earnings multiple by roughly 44%.

Second — and this is the single most consequential number in the file — the input carries a "live correction" asserting **net cash of EUR 2.02 billion** as "a genuine sum-of-the-parts add-back." That figure is cash and short-term investments of EUR 3,313 million less total debt of EUR 1,293 million. It is arithmetically correct and economically wrong, for two reasons. It ignores roughly EUR 750 million of restricted cash — the company's own disclosed net financial cash position excluding restricted cash is **EUR 1,270 million** at 2026-02-28, not EUR 2.02 billion. And even that EUR 1,270 million is overwhelmingly float: it sits against **EUR 4,076 million of other current liabilities**, the money owed to merchants and clients for vouchers issued but not yet redeemed. Working capital is EUR 191 million and the current ratio is 1.04. This is not a company sitting on a spare EUR 2 billion.

The chief financial officer made the distinction himself in April 2026, and it is the most important thing he said all year: he separated the "overall net cash position" from "what we call this net excess cash position, making a clear distinction between the contribution of float related cash... and this excess cash," and disclosed that **excess cash fell by about EUR 140 million in the first half** while the float-related position improved by EUR 240 million. Management does not treat the float as distributable. Neither should we.

The low Altman-Z solvency score of 1.0 in the screener is, as suspected, an artefact of this float-heavy balance sheet rather than a distress signal — S&P Global Ratings affirmed **BBB+/A-2 with a stable outlook on 2026-07-07**. Equally, the reported return on equity of 68% is an artefact of a EUR 393 million equity base, not evidence of an exceptional franchise; return on invested capital of 10.6% to 13.0% is the honest measure, and it is good rather than great.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Declining, and specifically declining on revenue while holding firm on margin.**

*October 2025 — offensive.* The language is expansionary and unqualified: "delivered above expectations across all key metrics," "we are clearly well ahead of our initial plan," "a step change in the group's financial profile." Management volunteered a EUR 100 million buyback and framed it as conviction: "we are aware of where the stock price is currently trading, and versus the value we consider we are able to create from this company."

*April 2026 — defensive on the top line, offensive on costs.* The hedges arrive in the opening remarks: "amid a more uncertain macro and geopolitical environment," "even if other products and services is facing temporary pressure in specific activities." The confident material has migrated entirely to the cost line — "structural cost efficiency," "accelerated automation, notably through the increasing use of AI as a key optimization enabler," "a clear prioritization of projects." When pushed by UBS on whether the reiterated EBITDA guide was conservative, the chief financial officer refused the easy answer and instead volunteered bad news: Brazil "will weigh a lot on the EBITDA margin of the group... in the second half of the year, we will face a lower EBITDA margin compared to the previous year."

That last exchange is the most creditable moment in either transcript. Management had an open invitation to sandbag and declined it.

The clearest tonal tell is the answer to UBS on why clients are shrinking their headcount. Asked directly whether the end-user decline was driven by artificial-intelligence-related hiring freezes, the chief executive did not deny it — he named the exposed sectors: "the automotive industry, the IT industry and part of the interim industry are currently under pressure." Pluxee's revenue is a function of how many employees its clients have. That is a demand channel management has now acknowledged it cannot control.

**Trajectory: Declining on growth confidence, Stable-to-Rising on operational confidence.**

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Medium-High. Management has consistently delivered or beaten what it controls, and has been early and honest about what it does not.**

The delivery record on internal targets is genuinely strong. Fiscal 2025 promised low-double-digit organic growth and delivered 10.6%. It promised roughly 150 basis points of margin expansion and delivered 230. It promised cash conversion above 75% on average and delivered 89%. New client development targeted EUR 1.3 billion and delivered EUR 1.5 billion. Each of these was checkable and each was met.

The failure is on the revenue guide, and it is large: fiscal 2026 went from high-single-digit organic revenue growth to **stable**. That is not a rounding error. But the cause is a sovereign regulator, it was flagged to investors at the half-year before it appeared in the numbers, and the fourth-quarter magnitude was pre-announced at roughly twice the third quarter's. Management did not let the market discover this.

Set against that, the screener records an earnings beat rate of **2 of 6 quarters (33%)** and consensus forward earnings growth of just **+0.3%**. The market has already stopped extrapolating.

There is one soft spot worth flagging. Management repeatedly guides to cash conversion "over 80% on average" and then stresses the word *over* — "we are not guiding on an 80% achievement, we are guiding on over 80%." That is a target constructed to be difficult to miss, on a metric that includes the float working-capital inflow. It is the one place where the disclosure is engineered rather than plain.

**Reliability: Medium-High.** High on margin, cost and cash. Medium on revenue, because the revenue is partly in the gift of legislators.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Four themes recur, and management engages seriously with three of them.

**The cash pile — pressed twice, answered evasively both times.** Deutsche Bank's Andre Juillard asked directly in April 2026: "Your cash net position is even stronger than what it was at the end of last year. Do you have any new plan about the use of this cash or still not clear?" The answer was that mergers and acquisitions remain "a key pillar," that the pipeline is "solid," and "we'll come back to you when it will be." In October 2025, the same analyst summarised the buyback answer as "the message is step by step," to which the chief financial officer replied "as always." Analysts are asking the exact right question — if the balance sheet is as strong as claimed, why is the return so small? — and are being deferred.

**Cross-selling — asked for numbers, given a direction.** Bernstein's Sabrina Blanc asked twice for the weight of non-meal-voucher solutions in operating revenue. She received: "the contribution coming from the cross-selling in percentage is higher than the overall growth." That is a ratio, not a level. Cross-selling is load-bearing in the medium-term story and remains unquantified.

**Cash conversion sustainability — pressed by Barclays, answered candidly.** Pravin Gondhale asked whether 90% conversion could persist. The chief financial officer explained that working capital swings with business growth and regulation, which is the honest answer and implicitly concedes the float dependency.

**Client headcount and artificial intelligence — raised by UBS, answered but not resolved.** This is the topic analysts pushed on that management is least able to address, because it is a second-order exposure: Pluxee does not lose clients, its clients lose employees. Net retention has already fallen to exactly 100% on this mechanism.

The topic no analyst pushed hard enough on, in either call, is what the Brazilian open-loop migration does to the structure of the business rather than to one year's revenue. That is the question that matters most and it went largely unasked.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **The Brazilian reform attacks the business model, not just the margin.** A 3.6% cap on the merchant discount rate compresses price. Migration to an open loop with a 2% regulated interchange fee from 2026-05-11 removes the closed network itself — the thing that made this a franchise rather than a card programme.

🔴 **Growth has come from price, and price is now regulated.** Management's own disclosure: 50 basis points of take-rate improvement over four years, "the vast majority... coming from the increase in the client commission." Volume growth, meanwhile, is negative at the end-user level.

🔴 **Net retention is at the floor, not above it.** 100% in fiscal 2025 and only "resilient" in the first half of fiscal 2026, with the end-user portfolio contribution having "turned negative" in the second half of fiscal 2025.

🔴 **Public-benefit programmes are a sovereign-budget derivative.** Romania and Austria suspended or reduced schemes "because of some budget constraints." This revenue line is exposed to European fiscal consolidation.

🔴 **The statutory cash flow is materially below the headline.** EUR 263 million trailing versus EUR 417 million on the company measure.

🔴 **Buyback is token relative to the claimed balance-sheet strength.** EUR 100 million against a EUR 2.14 billion market value — 4.7% — while management defers capital-return questions in favour of an unspecified acquisition pipeline.

🟢 **Margin execution is excellent and repeatable.** 229–268 basis points of organic expansion in the first half of fiscal 2026, on top of 230 in fiscal 2025, driven by a single platform architecture with genuine operating leverage.

🟢 **Business volume is still growing strongly even as revenue falls.** Third-quarter volume issued rose 9.4% organically to EUR 6.6 billion while revenue fell 3.3%. The customer franchise is intact; the price per unit is what regulation took.

🟢 **Investment-grade and unlevered.** S&P affirmed BBB+/A-2, stable, on 2026-07-07. Unlike its closest peer, Pluxee carries no net financial debt.

🟢 **Management pre-announced its own bad news.** The Brazil second-half margin hit was disclosed in April, before it appeared in any print.

🟢 **The third quarter landed better than feared** — the shares rose about 6% on the 2026-07-03 release, and the nine-month revenue figure still showed 2.7% organic growth.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**"Payment agnostic" is the tell.** In October 2025 management described the app's key strength as "being fully payment agnostic, it integrates the most popular digital payment options such as Google Pay, Apple Pay, and QR code solutions." That is presented as a feature. Read structurally, it is an admission that the proprietary payment rail — the closed loop — is no longer where the value sits. Brazil's regulator has now mandated exactly that outcome.

**The vocabulary migrated from acquisition to efficiency.** In October 2025 the recurring words are "new client development," "cross-selling," "face value." By April 2026 they are "operating leverage," "streamlining," "automation," "rigorous value creation monitoring." Artificial intelligence appears in both calls but in opposite roles: in October it is a customer-facing innovation ("AI-powered chatbots"); in April it is a cost lever ("a key optimization enabler") *and* a threat to clients' headcount. The same technology moved from the growth column to the cost column to the risk column in six months.

**"We are always very selective in this kind of program" is retrospective justification.** Applied to public benefits after governments cut them, it reframes a lost contract cycle as portfolio discipline.

**The United Kingdom and United States exit is being pre-buried.** Described as "strategically refocusing" and "progressively exiting noncore, lower return activities," with the reassurance that they "account for less than 5% of group revenues" and "should return to a positive contribution from fiscal 2027." Two years after a spin-off, two developed markets are being wound back.

**The chief financial officer's float-versus-excess-cash disaggregation was unprompted.** He volunteered a distinction that makes the balance sheet look weaker. That is a mark of integrity — and it is also the single fact that dismantles the "EUR 2 billion of net cash" version of this investment case.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: PIVOTING.**

This is not a deteriorating business and it is not a compounder either. It is a well-run franchise executing a genuine pivot — from volume-and-price growth to efficiency and cash conversion — forced on it by regulators in its most profitable region. The operational execution is real: 37% EBITDA margins, 86% cash conversion, investment-grade and unlevered, and business volume still compounding at 9.4% while revenue falls.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: the balance sheet is not what the screening file says it is.** The investment case for Pluxee rests almost entirely on whether roughly EUR 1.27 billion of net financial cash — against a EUR 2.14 billion market value — is shareholders' money or merchants' money. The company's own chief financial officer says most of it is float, and the company's own behaviour agrees: a EUR 55 million dividend and a EUR 100 million buyback are what management believes it can safely return. Anyone underwriting this at "trades below net cash" is underwriting a number the company does not recognise. Size to an enterprise value that credits perhaps EUR 250–350 million of genuinely surplus cash, not EUR 2 billion.

**Economic moat: a regulatory-licence and two-sided-network moat, ERODING.**

The moat type is real and identifiable: a tax-advantaged benefit mandated or incentivised by governments, delivered through a closed two-sided network of employers and merchants where both sides face switching costs. It produced a near-duopoly with Edenred and a take rate management could push up 50 basis points over four years.

The width evidence says erosion, not strength. Return on invested capital is 10.6% to 13.0% — respectable, not fortress-grade. Gross margin is contracting. The take rate, the direct measure of pricing power, is now capped by statute in Brazil at 3.6% on the merchant side. Most decisively, the migration to an open loop with a regulated 2% interchange from 2026-05-11 dissolves the closed network in that market — it converts a proprietary rail into a card programme competing on general-purpose payment infrastructure. A high margin that is falling because a regulator capped the price is the textbook definition of an eroding moat, not a wide one.

**Secular threat: MATERIAL, not terminal — the force is payments disintermediation.**

The structural force is the replacement of proprietary closed-loop benefit networks by open, regulated, general-purpose payment rails with capped interchange. Brazil has done it. The European Union's broader direction on instant payments and interchange caps points the same way, and Italy, France and Romania have each already touched voucher economics.

It is material rather than terminal for one specific reason: the underlying *demand* is a tax-advantaged employee benefit created by legislation, and no regulator has moved to abolish the benefit itself. Employers still want it, employees still receive it, and volume is still growing at 9.4%. What is being taken is the take rate, not the market. Pluxee will still be here in ten years; the question is whether it earns 37% EBITDA margins or 25%.

**Cheapness: partly a fear print, partly a shrinking base — and mostly already recovered.** At EUR 15.60 the shares trade at about 11 times trailing earnings on a roughly 12% free cash flow yield, against a closest peer at about 14 times. That is a real but modest discount, and it is a discount driven by a shared regulatory shock that hit both companies — sector beta, not a mispricing unique to Pluxee. Critically, the fear print has largely been paid: the shares are 57% above their 52-week low of EUR 9.905, 27% above their 200-day average, and sit essentially **on top of the analyst consensus target of about EUR 16.60**. The washed-out price was available in the spring. It is not available now.

Management credibility 3 of 5 · trajectory turning · a moat that is being eroded · moat trend eroding · structural threat material.
